candidates.source_body_excerpt: Seventeen people have been arrested as police tackle a “spider web of criminality” in Heywood and Rochdale. This morning, 250 officers carried out a series of raids as part of Operation Rivercrest which is targeting an organised crime group. The operation led to the execution of 20 warrants – mostly in Rochdale and Heywood – as well as in areas across Bury, Salford, Manchester, Merseyside and Yorkshire. Those arrested range in age from 19 to 49. Sixteen men have been arrested on suspicion of various offences, including drugs supply, assault, violent disorder, affray, burglary, and robbery. One woman, aged 21, was arrested on suspicion of being concerned in the supply of drugs. DS Hannah Taala, of Greater Manchester Police’s Rochdale Division, said officers focused on the crime group after violence in Heywood earlier in the year . She said: “There was a large disorder in April, where multiple people were involved in violence in the Heywood area. “It ended in some quiet serious injuries, assaults, a stab wound, using vehicles in that disorder, weapons, machetes. A cannabis farm was discovered during the raids. Image: GMP

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Two men from Rochdale are among 10 people charged with conspiracy to supply controlled drugs and conspiracy to supply an unauthorised medicinal product. The charges related to a seven-month long investigation by Greater Manchester Police’s Serious and Organised Crime Group into suspected large-scale supply and distribution of illicit drugs in Greater Manchester and West Midlands. Shakil Ahmed, 51,of Whittaker Lane, Rochdale, and Jailil Ahmed, 53, of Twinegate, Rochdale, have been charged with conspiracy to supply controlled drugs (Class A, B and C) and conspiracy to supply an unauthorised medicinal product, along with Daniyal Ahmed, 23, of no fixed abode; Raja Adeel Farooq, 44 of Kingsway, Burnage; Clayton Brown, 61, of Penn Road, Wolverhampton; Amarjit Mahay, 54, of Dudding Road, Wolverhampton; Samuel McConnell, 38, of Wrottesley Road West, Wolverhampton; Noel Streete, 59, of Old Stafford Road, Wolverhampton; Sheline Streete, 41, of Stephens Close, Wolverhampton; and a 16-year-old boy who cannot be named for legal reasons. They have been remanded in custody ahead of a scheduled appearance at Manchester Crown Court on Friday, November 13. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Final preparations are being made for the big Christmas lights switch-on in Middleton. Festive lights are already appearing across the town, including the return of the special red shoe outside Middleton Library in tribute to Rochdale Council officer Lauren Mason, who died suddenly two years ago. Lights and other decorations are being put up ahead of the big switch-on which takes place on Saturday, November 14, in Middleton Gardens. There are plenty of performances to get people into the festive spirit From 12pm, attractions include food and drinks, fairground rides and market stalls featuring the Teenage Market which supports local young entrepreneurs. The Art House will be offering personalised Christmas card making and there will also be face painting. Visitors to the town centre will also enjoy performances from community groups before Middleton Brass Band helps get people into the festive spirit from 4.30pm. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Residents across the borough will have the chance to come together to pay their respects to those who have served and made sacrifices for the defence and posterity of the country at Remembrance Day services. Commemorations will be held on Remembrance Sunday on the 8th November, with services and parades taking place across townships. Representatives from the Navy, Army, and Royal Air Force will join veterans and civil dignitaries for parades in Rochdale, Castleton, Heywood, Littleborough, Middleton, Milnrow, Norden, and Wardle. Members of the public are invited, and encouraged, to attend to show their gratitude to servicemen and women, past and present. Mayor of Rochdale, Councillor Faisal Rana, said: "Across the community we will come together on Sunday 8 November to pay tribute to our Armed Forces and honour the service and sacrifice of thousands of men and women. In our remembrance we honour the fallen, people of all faiths and no faith, from Heywood, Middleton, Pennines, and Rochdale. “The council supports all members of our Armed Forces community, young and old. We will always be there for them and their families. We are united in our remembrance, as all ages come together at local war memorials to reflect and remember, to pause and pray. Lest we forget.” The Royal British Legion is holding its annual poppy appeal until Sunday 8th November, raising money to support British servicemen and women and their families. Poppies can be bought online at www.britishlegion.org.uk at Number One Riverside, Rochdale, and selected places across the borough. For details of Remembrance Sunday services, times, and parades, visit www.rochdale.gov.uk/events

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Foster carers who have between them clocked up a total of 465 years supporting children and young people across the borough have been recognised by Rochdale Council. A total of 34 fostering families were honoured at the council’s recent annual Foster Carer Celebration Awards at Rochdale Town Hall in gratitude for their outstanding commitment to providing safe, stable and nurturing homes for some of the most vulnerable. Between all the carers, it is estimated they have supported more than 1,020 children and young people from newborn to 18, while working with the local authority. Among those celebrating their individual milestones was Michael, aged 79, and Marilyn, aged 75, who are marking 50 years. Predominantly caring for newborn babies and siblings since 1976, the married couple from Milnrow have cared for more than 330 children in that time and are still welcoming youngsters into their home. Marilyn said: “We’ve been to their weddings, adoption parties, christenings, 18th and 21st birthday parties. “It’s lovely when you think you started off with them as a baby and now, they’ve grown. Ian and Carole McLean celebrate 40 years of fostering with Rochdale Council “We’ve had letters from adoptive parents saying, ‘They’ve turned out like they have because of you’ which is nice.”

candidates.source_body_excerpt: I'm really pleased to be able to provide this update having been re-appointed as Chair of the Representative Body at last week's meeting. I'd like to welcome colleague Representative Rachael Ray as the new Deputy Chair and all the new Representatives who were attending their first meeting. I also want to say thank you to outgoing Deputy Chair Rob Dyson for all his hard work in the role. I am looking forward to working with all Representatives, new and returning, over the coming year. At the meeting, Representatives approved RBH's Annual Report To Customers. You can read the report in full on the RBH website . I'm really pleased that as Representatives we were able to provide some extra oversight from both customer and colleague Representatives before the report was published. We also approved the findings of our most recent scrutiny review. Representatives continue to use our scrutiny powers to help improve our services and communities. Over the past two years, Representative Body recommendations have helped to improve how we deal with complaints, how we gain access to carry out essential safety checks, our approach to anti-social behaviour, how we allocate and let our homes, how the repairs team communities with our customers, and how we manage sub-contractors. This recent review looked at how we can encourage customers to provide feedback about our investment programme. I'm really pleased that six of our seven recommendations have been accepted, including making sure in future that the way we ask for feedback is tailored to the needs of different customers. You can read more about the review on the RBH website , and I want to say thank you to all the panel members who worked so hard on the review, and also all the RBH team members who took the time to help. Finally, I want to remind you that being a Member of RBH means becoming part of something bigger. It offers you the opportunity to have a real voice in shaping the services we deliver, influencing decisions that affect your home, workplace, and community, and helping RBH continue to improve and grow. If you're not already a member, it only takes a few moments at www.rbh.org.uk/join to sign up, and I encourage you to do so. Membership strengthens our organisation. It ensures that RBH continues to listen, respond, and act in ways that reflect the needs and experiences of the people we serve and work alongside. I'm excited for the year ahead and what we can achieve together. Andrew Johnson Chair of the Representative Body

While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Claire Lord sits alone in her living room surrounded by head-high boxes. The small space between her sofa and TV is the only bit of the flat not crowded by cubes of clutter. To answer the door she has to clamber over yet more plastic tubs filled to the brim with her worldly possessions. The 56-year-old is ready to move out of her flat in Rochdale ’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks. She’s been ready for weeks. Claire was one of 229 households told they had to leave by landowners Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) in October 2025. Since then, droves have been moving out of the blocks. Only an estimated 90 households are still left in Seven Sisters - actually named College Bank. RBH says this has been done for safety reasons. The tower blocks face an uncertain future, with the question of demolition or refurbishment still on the table after a decade of limbo. No matter the decision, it is understood all residents will have to move out whilst work is done - whether that work is to decorate or destroy. Claire is one of the latest to be exiting the estate, but it’s not a move she really wanted to do. When describing the day when RBH told her they'd found some new digs for her, she said she was ‘gutted’. The security, the views, proximity to healthcare professionals and the community are the things she cherishes most about her flat. Claire will be moving to a bungalow across the road, behind Lidl. “There has been a delay because the lady who lived in the bungalow hadn't done work on the place for some time,” Claire explained. “They’ve had to do painting and decorating, rewiring, putting new doors on and a fresh kitchen. “So they’ve been getting it ready for me. RBH told me about four months ago that I’d be moving and were waiting for the date. “Every time I’ve gone down they’ve come up with more work and more work to do. I’ve been down every week to ask. “It’s always the same story - ‘something is being done’. I’ve still not got a move-in date, I think I’ll be told about a move-in date in four weeks. “I do love living here. The security is good and there isn’t much chance of you getting burgled. “It’s close to the shops in the town centre, my mental health team is nearby and my GP is just down the road. “But my biggest fear of moving is losing that security. I’ve been here (in Mardyke block) for 12 years and I've never had any trouble, it’s a good community. “If I could stay I would. It’s not good for my mental health. I don’t know whether I’m coming or going. “Being stuck halfway is no good as I just don’t know. They’re just going to plonk a day on me.” Claire has credited RBH with supporting her through the transition. She has regular contact with housing officers, but that doesn’t mean the transition process has been easy for her. Like many of the tenants, she just wants to know what’s happening with the blocks. Claire added: “We’ve had so many rumours about what is happening. We’ve heard they’re bringing in migrants in; that three are staying up and four are coming down; then we’ve had that they’re all staying up; then we’ve had they’re all coming down and they’re building 250 houses. “Nothing is set in concrete and they won’t tell us. It’s all just rumours.” Her friend Christine Hartley, who has lived in the Tentercroft block for 14 years, hasn’t accepted any new accommodation from RBH. Recalling the experience, she said: “Mine was a textbook case. "Because I'd turned 50, I'd received my invitation for routine screening and went along without any concerns. candidates.source_body_excerpt: A six-bedroom HMO could be created above a restaurant in Littleborough. Abdul Ahad has applied to Rochdale Council to convert part of the first and second floors of 15 Todmorden Road in Littleborough from restaurant and storage into a six-bedroom HMO above the Bay of Bengal restaurant. The application is part retrospective as work has already been carried out to create two roof lights and install a window. In supporting documents submitted to the council, Build Design Services said: “The ground floor is occupied by an established restaurant and will remain in its existing use. “The upper floors are currently vacant and were previously used for office and storage purposes. The proposal seeks to bring these underused areas of the building back into productive use as residential accommodation. “The proposed HMO will provide six single-occupancy bedrooms for a maximum of six residents. Four bedrooms and a shared kitchen/living area will be provided at first-floor level, with a further two bedrooms and bathroom facilities at second-floor level. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Tyler Walton notched a double as on-song Accrington extended their unbeaten run to nine games in all competitions with an emphatic 5-0 win at Rochdale. The points were all but secured by half-time as John Doolan’s side fired home three impressive strikes before the break on the way to their biggest victory since March 2025. Dale were booed off after a fifth successive match without victory. Stanley grabbed the lead in the 14th minute when Josh Woods guided in a low effort from 20 yards out after home goalkeeper Sam Waller passed the ball straight to him. Walton then slipped a lovely pass through for Charlie Warren to lash a low strike in off the post from the edge of the box in the 38th minute. Walton arced a stunning angled strike over Waller from just inside the box in first-half stoppage time. The winger doubled his tally in the 51st minute when he knocked in the rebound after Joe Anderson’s shot was saved by Waller. Sub Alex Henderson sealed the rout in the 66th minute by finishing off a brilliant move from 10 yards out.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale council has raked in £2.88m from parking fines in the last three years. Data obtained from a Freedom of Information (FOI) request revealed that the local authority has generated just under £1m per year from 2023 to 2026. From a total of 90,644 parking charge notices (PCNs) issued for 2023, 2024 and 2025, the council gained £2.88m, with the highest earning year being 2025 with £990,256. The total value of PCNs was just over £5.6m, but the income is less due to people successfully challenging claims or costs of chasing fines. The town hall says all money generated from PCNs is then reinvested into the road network. This reinvestment could include fixing potholes, re-drawing on road markers or larger infrastructure projects. The local authority also pointed out PCNs are issued for safety reasons, such as making sure pavements have enough space for wheelchair users or to prevent blind spots at junctions. The FOI, submitted by the Local Democracy Reporting Service, also revealed the biggest hotspots in the borough where people get PCNs. Newgate, Yorkshire Street Central and Oldham Road Central were all the places with the highest number of PCNs distributed. Newgate: Number of PCNs – 790, total income: £54,920 Yorkshire St Central: Number of PCNs – 623, total income: £39,970

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say. Some 81 two, three-and four-bedroom homes are currently under construction on vacant land next to Rochdale’s Central Retail Park. This forms part of a wider scheme to create a connection between the train station and the town centre. The wider regeneration of the area around Rochdale railway station also involves the creation of a new public square in front of the station and 33 new apartments on a brownfield site on the corner of Maclure Road and Station Road. The train station in Rochdale was once a hub for industrial business generations ago, so the distance between the station and the town centre was purposeful separation. But as times changed, society changed and the station suddenly started transporting people, not goods. This is why there is an idea to improve access and avenues from the station and the main hub of the town. This 81-home development, known as John Rennie Place, in honour of the late Scottish Civil engineer who masterminded the Rochdale Canal, got under way in November last year, and is due for completion in December 2027. The project, approved years ago, was unlocked following a successful bid for £15m from the government’s Community Regeneration Partnerships Fund. The transformation has been on the cards for a long time, but the local authority struggled to get the investment until last year. The properties will be the first affordable net zero homes delivered as part of a housing scheme supported by the council. The local authority says the development is already delivering benefits to the local economy and community.
candidates.source_summary: A scheme which would transform the gateway into Rochdale is making significant progress, town hall bosses say.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Lodge Mill in Middleton was devastated by a fire six months ago. Now there is hope for its future thanks to some dedicated business owners, volunteers and one avid ice cream fan. In March, firefighters were called to the massive blaze that left businesses in tatters and left the historic mill a shell. Several businesses were based on the ground floor of the building, believed to be one of the oldest mills in Middleton. A children’s dance studio, an ice cream parlour, a tea room, a dog chiropractor business and the Engine House event space, which held weddings, functions and parties, were all lost in the fire. The former silk and cotton mill, on Townley Street, dates back to around 1850. It was bought by couple Martin Cove and Paula Hickey in 2019, who were working passionately to renovate the three floors above. The pair have since kickstarted a fundraising campaign to restore the building soon after the fire, because the mill was uninsurable. Martin and Paula said the blaze ’caused the almost total loss of the main mill structure’. “No one was injured, and for that we are incredibly thankful,” the couple said at the time of the fire. “But we are heartbroken at the loss of not only our beloved Lodge Mill, but also the homes of the many local businesses and the community space we had all built together. “The outpouring of love and compassion from the people of Middleton and the surrounding area has given us the strength to carry on.” The GoFundMe page has raised just over £7,000 since it was launched six months ago. Thanks to a group of keen volunteers, life has returned to the mill.
